title: What the GOP gerrymandering backfire means for 2028 | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

When President Donald Trump launched hisbrazen mid-decade redistricting gambitin Texas last year, he confidently declared that Republicans were “entitled to five more seats” in the Lone Star State.

Of course, the GOP wasn’t entitled to anything. And the midterms offered a swift reality check.

In last week’s election, the party lost 4 of the 5 Texas seats it gerrymandered for itself last year. But it wasn’t just Texas. Republicans havewon only 2 of the 15 districtsthey tried to rig for themselves, according to CNN’s redistricting tracker. One more seat, in Louisiana, is going to a runoff.

And all told, the gambit actuallycostthem seats, after the map they redrew in North Carolina spread the party too thin and allowed Democrats to flip at least a half-dozen GOP seats. Democrats were also able to win a handful of additional seats in California when they fought back with their own redraw.

There’s a prevailing narrative that Trump’s redistricting gambit backfired on the GOP — and pretty badly. But while there’s no question the plot was costly in 2026, it’s too early to say it won’t help Republicans over the long term.

How could that be? And what’s next in the redistricting battles?

We’re still waiting for some results — and there’s some subjectivity involved in how you count wins and losses when it comes to redistricted seats — but right now it’s clear Republicans actually lost seats from the ploy.

The GOP gained one seat in Texas and another in Tennessee. But Democrats are set to flip five seats in California, six or seven in North Carolina and three in Ohio. They also flipped two GOP districts in Texas and they have a narrow lead in a district in Tennessee that Republicans diluted to make another district more winnable.

So, all told, Republicans redrew 15 districts for themselves, compared to just five for Democrats. But if current results hold, Democrats could gain a net of 16 seats from the states that were redrawn in this redistricting fight.

(Democrats also gained a seat in Utah, due to a court-ordered redraw of that state’s map.)

There has been plenty of talk since the election about how all of these maps backfired on Republicans. But that’s not strictly true.

North Carolinaclearly backfired — at least in this election and at the congressional level — but other maps like Florida’s and Texas’ merely failed to live up to GOP hopes.

Republicans didn’t lose seats in Florida and Texas because they redrew the maps; they just didn’t win the ones they’d hoped.

Republicans still won 63% of Texas’ districts despite losing every statewide race. And in Florida, Republicans still won 71% of the districts even though the statewide contests were close.

There is a term for when a gerrymander backfires by spreading your voters too thin and allowing the other party to win a bunch of districts: a “dummymander.” That really only happened in North Carolina.

But in a twist, local Republicans that declined to go along with Trump’s gambit actually saved the GOP from itself in this election.

According to ananalysis from Decision Desk HQ, attempted Republican redraws could’ve jeopardized an additional district in South Carolina and six more in Indiana — leading to a potential wipeout in the Hoosier State.

Trump was furious with GOP state senators who voted against these maps. He targeted and unseated a number of Indiana state legislators in the primaries.

It turned out they were doing him a favor. They prevented two more dummymanders.

But even when it comes to these maps that failed or even backfired in 2026, it’s worth taking the long view.

Just because they didn’t work or even hurt this time doesn’t mean it will always be thus, or that the whole thing will have been a bust.

It’s quite possible — even likely — that in closer elections in 2028 and 2030, Republicans would win back many of those seats in North Carolina and pick off more of the ones they aimed for in Alabama, Florida, Ohio and Texas. A lot of these districts favored Trump by double-digits, after all.

If that does happen, the GOP would have gained a fair amount of seats from this process, in the end.

And the party would probably declare that to be worth it. After all, the current Democratic gains basically just mean thealready-huge new Democratic majoritywill be about 11 seats bigger — around 260-175 instead of around 250-185 seats.

As things stand, the redistricting process moved the median House district about two points to the right — so that it’sa district Trump won by about five pointsin 2024, rather than by three points.

That wasn’t enough to withstand the Democrats’ biggest popular vote win in half a century, but it should still help plenty long term.

That’s if things stay where they are.

But the newly empowered state-level Democrats could finish what Republicans started byredrawing some more maps— and bringing this whole process something closer to long-term parity.

After previously facing legal obstacles to redrawing maps in Maryland, New York and Virginia, Democrats could move forward with redraws ahead of the 2028 election that could hand them a significant number of new seats in those states.

Democrats could also draw new maps in states where theyjust landed “trifectas”of control — the governorship and both chambers of the state legislature. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley has already said hewould sign a billredrawing the state’s congressional map. Another possibility would seem to be Minnesota.

The GOP has far fewer apparent opportunities to draw more seats.

It could be dicey politically for Democrats to jump back into redrawing maps. But Republicans clearly started it and drew many more seats for themselves.

And if Democrats don’t take advantage of what opportunities they have, this whole exercise could still benefit the GOP — even though it clearly didn’t do Trump, the person who pushed it so hard in the first place, much good.
